User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: Good — this is the right time to get organized. Below I’ve put together (1) focused questions to ask Lisa Park, (2) a checklist of documents to bring to your meeting and to the hearing, (3) short scripts/points you can say in common hearing types, and (4) practical courtroom and testimony tips. Use or adapt these when you meet with Lisa or contact her.

Important: this is general preparation help, not legal advice. Your attorney (Lisa Park) should confirm which documents to bring, what to file, and what to say in court.

1) Key questions to ask Lisa Park
- Case status and next steps
  - Where exactly are we in the federal-court schedule (status conference, motion hearing, preliminary injunction, trial, etc.) and what deadlines should I expect?
  - What will be on the court calendar next and what should we prepare before that date?
- Evidence & documents
  - Which documents do you want me to bring to our next meeting and to the hearing?
  - Are there documents I should gather now that might be hard to obtain later?
  - Do we need to exchange exhibits with opposing counsel before the hearing? If so, what are the deadlines and format requirements?
- Legal theory & remedies
  - What legal claims are we asserting (breach of NDA, breach of contract, injunctive relief, damages)? What elements will we need to prove?
  - What remedies should we seek (specific performance, injunctive relief, monetary damages, attorneys’ fees)?
- Burden, evidence, and witnesses
  - What is our burden of proof and what specific evidence will be most persuasive?
  - Should I expect to testify? Who are the witnesses we need and should we subpoena documents/witnesses?
  - Do we need expert testimony or declarations?
- Hearing logistics & strategy
  - What will happen at the hearing (judge’s likely questions, time limits, format)? How should I present the facts?
  - Should I prepare an opening statement or a short factual summary? If so, can you help me draft it?
  - Are there settlement options we should consider now?
- Confidentiality & protective orders
  - Because this involves an NDA, should we file anything under seal or ask for a protective order?
  - If sensitive documents are in evidence, how will we handle confidentiality in filings/hearing?
- Procedural & local rules
  - Are there particular local rules (Western District of Washington / King County federal courthouse) we must follow (exhibit format, number of copies, ECF deadlines)?
  - Do I need to bring extra copies of exhibits for the judge/courtroom deputy/opposing counsel?
- Practicalities
  - Will I need to travel to court? When should I arrive?
  - What should I wear and how should I conduct myself in court?
  - Anything else you want me to prepare or draft (chronology, exhibit binder, witness statements)?

2) Document checklist — bring to your next meeting with Lisa (privileged ok)
- The original NDA/contract and any amendments, addenda, or side agreements
- All communications related to the NDA and performance: emails, texts, letters, messaging app screenshots (showing promises, admissions, or refusal to perform)
- Copies of anything you provided under the NDA (documents you disclosed) and proof of when/how they were shared
- Notices you sent (demand letters, cure notices) and any responses from the landlord
- Any rent/payment records, invoices, receipts, or proof of performance on your side
- Photos, inspection reports, maintenance records, or other evidence tied to the landlord’s nonperformance
- Evidence of damages (invoices for repairs, lost business, valuation, receipts)
- Court filings and docket entries (complaint, exhibits, motions, declarations, proposed orders) and any discovery responses you’ve received or served
- Witness contact info and short statements (emails from third parties, neighbor statements)
- A chronological timeline of events (one-page timeline helps)
- Any insurance correspondence or third-party reports
- Your notes about conversations/meetings (dates, attendees, summary)
- Identification and contact details for witnesses and potential experts
- Any public records or county documents (property records, code violations) if relevant

Document checklist — specifically for the hearing (ask Lisa to confirm)
- Finalized exhibit list and pre-marked exhibits as required by the court (paper or electronic per local rule)
- Copies of all exhibits: typically judge + opposing counsel + 1 for you (confirm required number)
- Proposed order(s) or proposed findings (if the judge expects them)
- Declaration(s) summarizing facts (if the court requires written statements)
- Copies of any motions being argued and the briefing index
- USB with electronic copies (PDFs) of exhibits and filings (labelled and organized)
- Court-required filings (and proof of service) showing timely compliance with local rules

3) What to say in the hearing — short scripts and pointers
Note: tailor to the hearing type. Practice with Lisa first.

- Status conference / calendar call (if that’s the next step)
  - Concise factual summary (1–2 sentences): “This is a dispute regarding a nondisclosure agreement between me and my former landlord. I will be seeking enforcement/relief because the landlord stopped performing required obligations and breached the agreement.”
  - Case status points: discovery completed? outstanding discovery? settlement discussions? proposed schedule.
  - Be ready to answer: estimated length of trial, number of witnesses, whether you consent to magistrate, and discovery needs.

- Motion hearing (e.g., motion to compel, motion for summary judgment, preliminary injunction)
  - If you speak, open with a 30–60 second factual summary and the specific relief requested.
  - Emphasize key admissible evidence: dates, documents, and what they show (don’t narrate everything).
  - Answer the judge’s questions directly; if you don’t know, say so and offer to have your attorney address it.
  - Example short factual statement: “Your Honor, the NDA required the landlord to [specific obligation]. On [date(s)] the landlord stopped [performance], and despite our demand on [date], they have not complied. The attached emails and the attached exhibit (Ex. 4) show this.”

- Preliminary injunction (if seeking immediate relief)
  - Be prepared to hit the four pillars succinctly: likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, balance of equities, and public interest.
  - Focus on immediate harm and urgency — concrete examples and damages or risk.
  - Bring strong documentary support and any sworn declarations.

- Trial (if you testify or attend)
  - Opening (if you testify): brief, factual timeline, avoid argument or speculation.
  - Testifying: tell the truth, remain calm, answer aloud directly and succinctly, avoid volunteering extra details.

4) Testimony & courtroom behavior tips
- If you testify:
  - Tell the truth. Keep answers short and responsive.
  - Pause and think before answering. If you don’t remember, say “I don’t recall” rather than guessing.
  - Don’t argue with opposing counsel. If you disagree, state the fact calmly.
  - Listen carefully to the whole question; ask for clarification if the question is confusing.
  - Don’t use slang or jokes; be professional and composed.

- General courtroom etiquette
  - Arrive early; bring ID and a quiet disposition.
  - Dress conservatively and professionally.
  - Address the judge as “Judge [LastName]” or “Your Honor.”
  - Turn off phone/silence it.
  - Follow Lisa’s lead about when you will speak.

5) Practical and procedural items Lisa will likely want to handle
- Exhibit numbering/marking, exhibit exchange deadlines, and courtesy copies for the judge
- Filing proposed orders or redacted/sealed filings if needed
- Preparing witness declarations or trial affidavits
- Subpoenas or third-party records requests (if necessary)
- Deposition scheduling or discovery motions if outstanding
- Confirming local rules for exhibit format and ECF filing procedures

6) Preparing a concise chronology and exhibit binder (do this now)
- Create a 1–2 page chronology: dates, short description of events, and references to exhibit numbers (e.g., “3/12/25 — Demand letter (Exhibit 2)”).
- Create an exhibit binder: tabbed exhibits in order, with an index and copies for Lisa, the court, and opposing counsel as required.

7) What I can do to help right now
- Draft a short email or list you can send to Lisa with the questions above.
- Help format your chronology and an exhibit index.
- Create a one-page script for what you’ll say in the hearing depending on which hearing it is (status conference vs. motion hearing vs. preliminary injunction).

Would you like me to:
- Draft an email to Lisa Park with these questions? or
- Make a one-page chronology and exhibit index template you can fill in?

Tell me which you prefer and any extra details you want included (dates, key documents you already have), and I’ll prepare it.
